Reproducing Seiler et al. (2022) from dandiset 000971¶

Paper. Seiler JL, Cosme CV, Sherathiya VN, Schaid MD, Bianco JM, Bridgemohan AS, Lerner TN (2022). Dopamine signaling in the dorsomedial striatum promotes compulsive behavior. Current Biology 32, 1175-1188. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2022.01.055. This attempt used the full text of the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC8930615). The supplementary figures could not be downloaded, so claims on Figures S1 to S7 rest on the main text.

Dandiset. DANDI:000971, version 0.261013.1707. The paper predates the dandiset and cites no version. This is the most recent published version. All three published versions (0.240802.2004, 0.260213.1851, 0.261013.1707) and the draft hold the same 4139 assets with the same blobs; they differ only in dandiset metadata (contributors, ORCIDs, study targets), none of which the analysis uses.

Code read. The authors' photometry code (GitHub jillianseiler/Seiler-et-al.-2022-MATLAB-code, commit 56f1529) and the conversion code with its notes (GitHub catalystneuro/lerner-lab-to-nwb, commit d301f7e). The photometry processing here follows the authors' code where the Methods are silent.

Outside inputs. One claim (Figure S3A-B) uses the densitometry table on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.11266654), which the dandiset names as its supplement.

import hashlib
import io
import time
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.multicomp import pairwise_tukeyhsd

import seiler

pd.set_option("display.width", 220)
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 40)
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 400)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=FutureWarning)

started = time.time()
sessions = seiler.list_sessions()
print(f"{len(sessions)} assets in dandiset {seiler.DANDISET_ID} version {seiler.DANDISET_VERSION}")

# Each subject's experiment and arm, from its files other than the 'Unknown' DLS files.
named = sessions[(sessions.arm != "Unknown") & sessions.experiment.notna()]
subj_arm = named.groupby("subject").group.agg(lambda g: g.value_counts().index[0])
sessions["subject_group"] = sessions.subject.map(subj_arm)
sessions["subject_experiment"] = sessions.subject_group.str.extract(
    r"^(FP|Opto-DLS-Excitatory|Opto-DMS-Excitatory|Opto-DMS-Inhibitory)")[0]
sessions["subject_arm"] = sessions.subject_group.str.split("-").str[-1]

is_fp = sessions.subject_experiment == "FP"
is_opto = sessions.subject_experiment.str.startswith("Opto", na=False)
need = is_fp | (is_opto & sessions.stage.isin(["shock", "omission"])) | (
    sessions.subject_experiment.isin(["Opto-DMS-Excitatory", "Opto-DLS-Excitatory"]) & sessions.stage.isin(["FR1", "RI30"]))
# one file of every optogenetic subject, for its notes
need |= is_opto & ~sessions.subject.duplicated() & sessions.subject_experiment.notna()
to_load = sessions[need]
t = time.time()
events = seiler.read_all_events(to_load.asset_id.tolist())
print(f"read the events of {len(events)} files in {time.time() - t:.0f} s")

def event_hash(ev):
    h = hashlib.md5()
    for k in sorted(ev):
        h.update(k.encode())
        h.update(np.round(np.asarray(ev[k]), 3).tobytes())
    return h.hexdigest()

loaded = sessions[sessions.asset_id.isin(list(events))].copy()
loaded["hash"] = [event_hash(events[a]["events"]) if events[a]["events"] else "" for a in loaded.asset_id]
dups = loaded[(loaded.hash != "") & loaded.duplicated("hash", keep=False)].sort_values("hash")
pairs = dups.groupby("hash").agg(n=("path", "size"), subjects=("subject", "nunique"),
                                 groups=("group", lambda g: ",".join(sorted(set(g)))), stage=("stage", "first"),
                                 n_events=("asset_id", lambda a: sum(len(v) for v in events[a.iloc[0]]["events"].values())))
print("Loaded files whose event series are identical to another loaded file:", len(dups), "in", len(pairs), "sets")
print(pairs.groupby(["subjects", "groups", "stage"]).size().to_string())
exp_files = sessions[sessions.experiment.notna()]
same_start = exp_files[exp_files.duplicated(["subject", "start"], keep=False)]
print("\nFiles in the 'Unknown' DLS excitatory group:", int((sessions.arm == "Unknown").sum()))
print("All files sharing subject and start time with another file:", len(same_start),
      "; their groups:", same_start.group.value_counts().to_dict())
odd = pairs[pairs.subjects > 1]
for h in odd.index:
    d = dups[dups.hash == h]
    r = seiler.rewards(events[d.asset_id.iloc[0]]["events"])
    print("\nIdentical across subjects:", d.subject.tolist(), d.stage.iloc[0], "; reward intervals (s) from",
          np.round(np.diff(r).min(), 2), "to", np.round(np.diff(r).max(), 2), "; series:", list(events[d.asset_id.iloc[0]]["events"]))

The 'Unknown' DLS excitatory files repeat sessions of the same mice that are also deposited under their named arm, with the same start time and identical events; each such session is counted once below (the named copy is kept). The omission probes identical across three mice hold only reward times, at the 20 s spacing the omission schedule gives a mouse that never nosepokes, so they are consistent with three mice that did not respond, not with one file deposited three times.

The fiber photometry mice carry their phenotype in two places, the file names and the notes, and the two agree. RR20 mice are labelled 'Punishment Sensitive' in the notes; the paper does not classify RR20 mice. Optogenetic mice have no stored phenotype, so they are classified here by the Methods rule.

side_rows = []
for a, r in ok_loaded.set_index("asset_id").iterrows():
    if not isinstance(r.side, str) or r.stage not in ("FR1", "RI30", "RI60", "RR20", "shock"):
        continue
    ev = events[a]["events"]
    rw = seiler.rewards(ev)
    if len(rw) == 0:
        continue
    def frac(s):
        p = ev.get(f"{s}_nose_poke_times", np.array([]))
        return np.isin(np.round(rw, 2), np.round(p, 2)).mean() if len(p) else 0.0
    other = "left" if r.side == "right" else "right"
    series = "+".join(k.split("_")[0] for k in ("left_reward_times", "right_reward_times") if k in ev)
    side_rows.append({"stage": r.stage, "described_side": r.side, "reward_series": series,
                      "rewards_in_described_side_pokes": frac(r.side) > 0.9, "rewards_in_other_side_pokes": frac(other) > 0.9})
side_df = pd.DataFrame(side_rows)
print("Do reward times coincide with nosepokes on the side the session description names? (files with rewards)")
print(side_df.groupby(["stage", "described_side", "reward_series", "rewards_in_described_side_pokes",
                       "rewards_in_other_side_pokes"]).size().to_string())

In training and probe sessions the reward times coincide with nosepokes on the side the description names. In shock probes on the left side the reward series is stored as right_reward_times while its times are left nosepokes, so the series name is wrong there; rewards are taken from either series. In most RR20 files the reward times do not coincide with any nosepoke time (MedPC delivers the RR reward after the counted nosepoke); RR20 files are used here only for reward counts and probes.

probe_files = ok_loaded[ok_loaded.stage == "shock"]
chk = []
for a in probe_files.asset_id:
    ev = events[a]["events"]
    if "footshock_times" not in ev:
        continue
    sh, rw = ev["footshock_times"], seiler.rewards(ev)
    chk.append({"n_shock": len(sh), "n_rew": len(rw), "shock_at_reward": np.isin(np.round(sh, 2), np.round(rw, 2)).mean() if len(sh) else np.nan,
                "first5_unshocked": not np.isin(np.round(rw[:5], 2), np.round(sh, 2)).any(), "last_event_s": max(v.max() for v in ev.values() if len(v))})
chk = pd.DataFrame(chk)
print(f"Shock probe files with footshock_times: {len(chk)} of {len(probe_files)}")
print(f"Fraction of shocks at a reward time: median {chk.shock_at_reward.median():.2f}, min {chk.shock_at_reward.min():.2f}")
ratio = chk.n_shock / chk.n_rew.replace(0, np.nan)
print(f"Shocks per reward: median {ratio.median():.2f} (Methods: RR3, about 1/3); 5th to 95th percentile {ratio.quantile(.05):.2f} to {ratio.quantile(.95):.2f}")
print("First five rewards never shocked (Methods):", int(chk.first5_unshocked.sum()), "of", len(chk))
print(f"Last event time in probe files: up to {chk.last_event_s.max():.0f} s (Methods: 60 min or 10 min of inactivity)")

Every shock falls on a rewarded nosepoke, about one reward in three is shocked, and the first five rewards are never shocked, as the Methods describe. Sessions hold at most 50 rewards and end within about an hour, consistent with the Methods' one hour or 50 rewards; the exception is an RI60 file whose last event is at 5354 s, which may be one of the sessions the conversion notes say were stitched from two recordings. Times are in seconds from the session start.

Shock probes come in the order the Results give, the early one after 0 to 4 RI60 (or RR20) sessions (median 1) and the late one after 11 to 18 (median 13). Two probe days have two files that both hold shocks; the last of the day is used, and the sum is a variant. Five mice lack a probe in the dandiset: two PR mice (028.392, 62.207) and one RR20 mouse have no late probe, and one PR mouse (89.247) and one PS mouse (78.214) have no early probe. For 89.247 a photometry session one day after its first RI60 session is deposited as a 'Probe Test' session with no footshock series. 32 RI60 mice and 5 RR20 mice have both probes.

all_ph = fp[fp.asset_id.map(lambda a: events[a]["has_photometry"])]
print("Files with photometry by stage:", all_ph.stage.value_counts().to_dict())
fp_sessions = all_ph[all_ph.stage.isin(["RI60", "RR20"])].sort_values("start_ts").copy()
fp_first_probe = fp_probes.sort_values("date").groupby("subject").date.first()
ri60_dates = fp[fp.stage.isin(["RI60", "RR20"])].groupby("subject").date.apply(sorted)
fp_sessions["train_day"] = [sum(d < r.date for d in ri60_dates.get(r.subject, [])) + 1 for r in fp_sessions.itertuples()]
early_probe = fp_probes[fp_probes.probe == "early"].set_index("subject").date
fp_sessions["fp_stage"] = [
    ("early" if r.date < early_probe[r.subject] else "late") if r.subject in early_probe.index
    else ("early" if r.train_day <= 3 else "late") for r in fp_sessions.itertuples()]
fp_sessions = fp_sessions.merge(fp_subj[["subject", "pheno", "behavior"]], on="subject")
print("Photometry sessions:", len(fp_sessions), "from", fp_sessions.subject.nunique(), "mice")
print(pd.crosstab([fp_sessions.pheno, fp_sessions.stage], fp_sessions.fp_stage).to_string())
print("\nMice with photometry per phenotype and stage (paper Fig 3E: RI30 PR 6, DPR 6, PS 11; early PR 7, DPR 9, PS 15; late PR 5, DPR 6, PS 13):")
print(fp_sessions.groupby(["pheno", "fp_stage"]).subject.nunique().unstack().to_string())

def process_photometry(row):
    rec = seiler.load_photometry(row.asset_id)
    d, fs, t0, ev = rec["data"], rec["fs"], rec["t0"], rec["events"]
    rew, unrew = seiler.split_nosepokes(ev, row.side)
    def inside(times):  # events whose PSTH window lies inside the recording (as seiler.psth)
        idx = np.round((np.asarray(times) - t0) * fs)
        return int(((idx - seiler.PSTH_PRE_S * fs >= 0) & (idx + seiler.PSTH_POST_S * fs < len(d))).sum())
    out = {"asset_id": row.asset_id, "fs": fs, "t0": t0, "n_samples": len(d), "duration_s": len(d) / fs,
           "last_event_s": max((v.max() for v in ev.values() if len(v)), default=np.nan),
           "n_rewards": len(seiler.rewards(ev)), "locations": ",".join(rec["locations"]),
           "sources": ",".join(s.split("_")[-1] for s in rec["sources"]),
           "n_rewarded": len(rew), "n_unrewarded": len(unrew),
           "n_rewarded_kept": inside(rew), "n_unrewarded_kept": inside(unrew), "coordinates": str(np.round(rec["coordinates"], 2).tolist()),
           "modulation": ";".join(f"{k.replace('commanded_voltage_series_', '')}={v:g}" for k, v in sorted(rec["modulation_hz"].items()))}
    for region, (si, ci) in {"DMS": (0, 1), "DLS": (2, 3)}.items():
        out[f"{region}_dropout_frac"] = seiler.dropout_mask(d[:, si], d[:, ci], fs).mean()
        z = seiler.zscored_dff(d[:, si], d[:, ci], fs)
        res = seiler.peak_score(z, fs, rew, unrew, t0)
        out[f"{region}_score"], out[f"{region}_rew_max"], out[f"{region}_unrew_min"] = res["score"], res["rew_max"], res["unrew_min"]
        out[f"{region}_psth_rew"], out[f"{region}_psth_unrew"] = res["psth_rew"], res["psth_unrew"]
        out[f"{region}_auc_2_10"] = res["auc_2_10"]
        # the authors' processing without the dropout step
        z0 = seiler.zscored_dff(d[:, si], d[:, ci], fs, mask_dropouts=False)
        out[f"{region}_score_nomask"] = seiler.peak_score(z0, fs, rew, unrew, t0)["score"]
        out[f"{region}_max_abs_z_nomask"] = np.nanmax(np.abs(z0))
        # clock check: the same events shifted by 37 s
        out[f"{region}_rew_max_shifted"] = seiler.peak_score(z, fs, rew + 37.0, unrew + 37.0, t0)["rew_max"]
        # column check: the channels the other way round
        zs = seiler.zscored_dff(d[:, ci], d[:, si], fs)
        out[f"{region}_rew_max_swapped"] = seiler.peak_score(zs, fs, rew, unrew, t0)["rew_max"]
    out["t_psth"] = res["t"]
    return out


t = time.time()

    print(f"{region} sessions excluded for dropouts over 10% of samples:", ph.loc[bad, ["subject", "date"]].to_dict("records"))

The dandiset holds photometry for RI60 and RR20 training sessions only (and one session described as a probe test, not used): none for RI30 and none for the shock probes, though the Methods say recordings were made during RI30 and on both probes. Early sessions are on the first to third RI60 day and late ones on days 12 to 18. The files label the four columns DMS 465 nm, DMS 405 nm, DLS 465 nm and DLS 405 nm, with the modulation frequencies the Methods give (211 and 330 Hz for DMS, 450 and 270 Hz for DLS). The stored fiber coordinates lose the signs the Methods give (DV 2.8 for -2.8, DLS AP 0.1 for -0.1). The authors' code comments call the first column of each pair the control and the second the signal; the data side with the files: the rewarded nosepoke response computed as labelled is larger than with the two channels swapped in most sessions (printed above). The response is above that for the same events shifted by 37 s in most sessions of both regions, so the behavioral events and the photometry share a clock. The DLS response has the larger area 2 to 10 s after the nosepoke, matching the prolonged DLS component the Results describe, which is consistent with the region labels; it does not prove them. In one session (332.393, 2020-07-28) the reward times are MedPC times that do not coincide with any nosepoke time, which are TDT times, so it has no rewarded nosepokes and no score. The DLS channels of one session (141.308, 2019-08-09) drop out so often that, with 1 s around each dropout, 99.97% of its samples are left out; that DLS recording is excluded. Some recordings are shorter than their behavioral session, by up to 2257 s; events whose PSTH window leaves the recording are dropped, which removes 1 of 2337 rewarded and 24 of 10916 unrewarded nosepokes. Only one session keeps under 90% of either kind (92.246 on 2019-02-27, 69 of 85 unrewarded). Some recordings hold dropouts where a raw channel falls near zero, which give |z| above 1000 without the dropout step.

def mixed_anova(df, between, within="probe", dv="shocks", subject="subject"):
    """Two-way mixed ANOVA (one between, one within factor of two levels), complete cases."""
    w = df.pivot_table(index=[subject, between], columns=within, values=dv).dropna().reset_index()
    levels = [c for c in w.columns if c not in (subject, between)]
    a, b = w[levels[0]].to_numpy(), w[levels[1]].to_numpy()
    g = w[between].to_numpy()
    groups = pd.unique(g)
    n, k = len(w), len(groups)
    mean_subj = (a + b) / 2
    grand = mean_subj.mean()
    ss_between = 2 * sum(((mean_subj[g == x].mean() - grand) ** 2) * (g == x).sum() for x in groups)
    ss_subj_err = 2 * sum(((mean_subj[g == x] - mean_subj[g == x].mean()) ** 2).sum() for x in groups)
    d = b - a
    ss_time = n * (d.mean() ** 2) / 2
    ss_inter = sum((g == x).sum() * (d[g == x].mean() - d.mean()) ** 2 for x in groups) / 2
    ss_within_err = sum(((d[g == x] - d[g == x].mean()) ** 2).sum() for x in groups) / 2
    df_b, df_e = k - 1, n - k
    out = {}
    for name, ss, dfn, sse in [(between, ss_between, df_b, ss_subj_err), (within, ss_time, 1, ss_within_err),
                               (f"{between} x {within}", ss_inter, df_b, ss_within_err)]:
        F = (ss / dfn) / (sse / df_e)
        out[name] = {"F": F, "df": f"{dfn},{df_e}", "p": stats.f.sf(F, dfn, df_e)}
    return pd.DataFrame(out).T, w


def fmt(aov):
    return aov.assign(F=aov.F.map("{:.2f}".format), p=aov.p.map("{:.2g}".format)).to_string()


def tukey(values, groups):
    t = pairwise_tukeyhsd(np.asarray(values, float), np.asarray(groups))
    return pd.DataFrame(t._results_table.data[1:], columns=t._results_table.data[0])

Training sessions kept: 551

The 20 RR20 files without rewards or nosepokes hold port entries only, so their nosepokes and rewards are not in the dandiset; they come from four RR20 mice over the same five days. The PS file of 140.306 ends after 170 s, holds 30 events (inactive nosepokes and port entries) with no active nosepoke and no reward, and is followed the same day by a full session of 50 rewards. The rule that leaves these 21 files out of the training measures is no active nosepoke and no reward. It was set after the first round of verification. A false start is a reason that fits some kept files as well (271.396 with 2 rewards in 720 s, 88.239 with 1 reward on two days, 92.246 with 4, 348.393 and 115.273 with 3), which hold active nosepokes and rewards and so are kept by the rule. The sections of fig2c, fig2n and figs1i also give the result with the 21 files kept.

Ten other mouse-days hold two or three RI60 files. Most pair a short file of 1 to 7 rewards with a full session, but some do not (81.236 on 2019-02-06 has files of 6, 28 and 42 rewards). Each file counts as a session here, as the dandiset deposits them; fig2c and fig2n also give the result with one file per mouse-day, the one with the most rewards.

fig1d-ri60-vs-rr20-shocks¶

Mice trained on RI60 accept more shocks in the shock probes than mice trained on RR20 (main effect of schedule, F1,43 = 6.37, p < 0.05; schedule by time interaction, F1,43 = 4.54, p < 0.05), and RI60 mice accept more shocks on the late probe than on the early one (p < 0.01).

In [12]:
def fig1d(long):
    aov, w = mixed_anova(long, "behavior")
    ri = w[w.behavior == "RI60"]
    t_ = stats.ttest_rel(ri["late"], ri["early"])
    return aov, w, t_

aov, w, t_ = fig1d(fp_long)
print(fmt(aov))
print(w.groupby("behavior")[["early", "late"]].agg(["mean", "std", "size"]).round(2).to_string())
print(f"RI60 late vs early: paired t = {t_.statistic:.2f}, p = {t_.pvalue:.2g}, Bonferroni x2 p = {min(1, 2 * t_.pvalue):.2g}")
rr = w[w.behavior == "RR20"]
print(f"RR20 late vs early: paired t p = {stats.ttest_rel(rr['late'], rr['early']).pvalue:.2g} (n = {len(rr)})")
aov_s, w_s, t_s = fig1d(fp_long_sum)
print("\nVariant, shocks summed over a probe day's files:"); print(fmt(aov_s)); print(
      f"RI60 late vs early Bonferroni p = {min(1, 2 * t_s.pvalue):.2g}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 3))
for sched, c in [("RI60", "k"), ("RR20", "grey")]:

    ax.plot([0, 1], [d.early.mean(), d.late.mean()], c, lw=3, label=f"{sched} (n={len(d)})")
ax.set_xticks([0, 1], ["early", "late"]); ax.set_ylabel("shocks"); ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("Plotted counts span", w[["early", "late"]].min().min(), "to", w[["early", "late"]].max().max())

Result: not reproduced. In the 32 RI60 and 5 RR20 mice with both probes, RI60 mice accept more shocks on average (early 11.38, late 16.31, against 4.80 and 6.60), but the schedule effect has p = 0.071 (F1,35 = 3.46) and the interaction p = 0.59. The RI60 increase from early to late has paired p = 0.032, which is 0.063 after the Bonferroni correction, above the claim's 0.01. The dandiset holds 6 RR20 mice, 5 with both probes, where Figure 1D has 9. Summing a probe day's files changes none of this.

fig1e-omission-ri60-longer¶

RI60-trained mice take longer to complete the omission probe than RR20-trained mice (unpaired t-test, p < 0.05; n = 20 and 7).

Result: partially reproduced. RI60 mice take 33.97 min to complete the omission probe (n = 19) and RR20 mice 17.72 min (n = 4); the unpaired t-test gives p = 0.070, so the direction holds without significance. The RR20 times vary little (SD 1.05, a variance 251 times smaller than RI60's), and a Welch test gives p = 0.0005. The dandiset holds 4 RR20 omission probes where the paper has 7, and 19 RI60 ones where it has 20.

fig1f-omission-shock-no-correlation¶

Among RI60 mice, shocks received on the late probe and omission completion time are not significantly correlated (r = 0.42, ns).

In [14]:

r1 = stats.pearsonr(o1.late, o1.omission_min)
print(f"Pearson r = {r1.statistic:.3f}, p = {r1.pvalue:.3g}, n = {len(o1)}")
o1e = fp_el[(fp_el.schedule == "RI60")].dropna(subset=["omission_min", "early"])
print(f"Variant, early probe: r = {stats.pearsonr(o1e.early, o1e.omission_min).statistic:.3f}, p = {stats.pearsonr(o1e.early, o1e.omission_min).pvalue:.3g}, n = {len(o1e)}")
print(f"Spearman, late probe: rho = {stats.spearmanr(o1.late, o1.omission_min).statistic:.3f}, p = {stats.spearmanr(o1.late, o1.omission_min).pvalue:.3g}")

Pearson r = 0.335, p = 0.175, n = 18
Variant, early probe: r = 0.592, p = 0.0076, n = 19
Spearman, late probe: rho = 0.403, p = 0.097

Result: reproduced. Late probe shocks and omission time are not significantly correlated (r = 0.335, p = 0.175, n = 18; the paper gives r = 0.42, ns). With the early probe the correlation is significant (r = 0.592, p = 0.0076, n = 19).

fig2a-phenotype-rule¶

RI60 mice are split by their shock probe counts into 9 PR, 9 DPR and 18 PS mice, by the rule in the Methods (DPR when the count rises by more than 85%; otherwise PR when the early count exceeds 13).

Result: partially reproduced. The stored labels count 9 PR, 9 DPR and 18 PS, as in Figure 2A. These counts are the stored labels, so they match by construction; the informative check is the rule. The Methods rule gives the stored label for 31 of the 32 mice with both probes; mouse 048.392 has 13 shocks on its early probe and a 38.5% rise, so the rule ("more than 13") makes it PS, while it is stored as PR. With PR at 13 or more all 32 agree. The 85% cut matches the top quartile of change here (75th percentile 87.7%), but the median early count is 9.0, not 13, so the "median split" at 13 is not a median of these mice.

Result: partially reproduced. PS mice earn 39.12 rewards per RI60 session, DPR 44.98 and PR 44.66, all within tolerance of 39.91, 46.56 and 45.33, and the ANOVA has p = 0.028 (F = 4.02), but Tukey PS vs DPR gives p = 0.059. The result sits at the threshold: with the false start of 140.306 kept as a session of 0 rewards, Tukey p is 0.048, and with one file per mouse-day (means PS 39.98, DPR 46.16, PR 44.66) it is 0.044. The rule used, no active nosepoke and no reward, was set after the first round of verification and is the only one of the three that gives p above 0.05. The other short files of 1 to 4 rewards, which the one-file-per-mouse-day variant drops, fit its false-start reason as well. The claim should be read as borderline.

Fiber photometry cohort: dopamine axon signals¶

fig3e-ri30-dms-peaks¶

Peaks in DMS dopamine axon activity at rewarded nosepokes emerge during RI30 in PR mice, and more slowly across RI60 in DPR mice.

Blocked: the dandiset holds photometry only for RI60 and RR20 sessions (and one session labelled as a probe test), not for RI30, so the emergence of peaks during RI30 cannot be tested. The early and late RI60 PSTHs are shown in the data check above.

fig3f-dms-score-phenotype¶

The DMS rewarded-unrewarded peak score differs by phenotype (F2,33 = 8.16, p < 0.01) and changes across training (p < 0.001).

In [26]:
# One score per mouse and stage: the mean over its sessions in that stage (one mouse has two early sessions).
sc = ph[ph.pheno.isin(["PR", "DPR", "PS"])].groupby(["subject", "pheno", "fp_stage"])[
    ["DMS_score", "DLS_score", "DMS_score_nomask", "DLS_score_nomask"]].mean().reset_index()
print("Mice per phenotype and stage with a DMS score:")
print(sc.dropna(subset=["DMS_score"]).groupby(["pheno", "fp_stage"]).size().unstack().to_string())
print("Mice per phenotype and stage with a DLS score:")
print(sc.dropna(subset=["DLS_score"]).groupby(["pheno", "fp_stage"]).size().unstack().to_string())


def phenotype_model(df, col):
    d = df.dropna(subset=[col]).rename(columns={col: "y"})
    full = smf.mixedlm("y ~ C(pheno) * C(fp_stage)", d, groups=d.subject).fit(reml=False)
    no_ph = smf.mixedlm("y ~ C(fp_stage)", d, groups=d.subject).fit(reml=False)
    no_stage = smf.mixedlm("y ~ C(pheno)", d, groups=d.subject).fit(reml=False)
    lr_p = 2 * (full.llf - no_ph.llf)
    lr_s = 2 * (full.llf - no_stage.llf)
    out = {"n_obs": len(d), "n_mice": d.subject.nunique(),
           "phenotype_LR": lr_p, "phenotype_p": stats.chi2.sf(lr_p, 4),
           "stage_LR": lr_s, "stage_p": stats.chi2.sf(lr_s, 3)}
    for st in ["early", "late"]:
        s = d[d.fp_stage == st]
        out[f"anova_{st}_p"] = stats.f_oneway(*[s[s.pheno == g].y for g in ["PR", "DPR", "PS"] if (s.pheno == g).sum() > 1]).pvalue
    return out, d.groupby(["pheno", "fp_stage"]).y.agg(["mean", "std", "size"])

fig3e-ri30-dms-peaks, the RI60 part¶

The claim is blocked, as its RI30 part needs photometry that is not in the dandiset. Its second part, peaks growing more slowly across RI60 in DPR mice, can be looked at with the early and late RI60 scores. This does not decide an outcome.

In [28]:
d3e = sc.dropna(subset=["DMS_score"]).pivot(index=["subject", "pheno"], columns="fp_stage", values="DMS_score").reset_index()
print("DMS score by phenotype and stage (all mice with that stage):", sc.groupby(["pheno", "fp_stage"]).DMS_score.mean().round(2).unstack().to_dict("index"))
for g in ["PR", "DPR", "PS"]:
    x = d3e[(d3e.pheno == g)].dropna(subset=["early", "late"])
    if len(x) > 1:
        print(f"{g}: {len(x)} mice with both stages, early {x.early.mean():.2f}, late {x.late.mean():.2f}, change {np.mean(x.late - x.early):.2f}, paired t p = {stats.ttest_rel(x.late, x.early).pvalue:.2g}")
    else:
        print(f"{g}: {len(x)} mice with both stages")

DMS score by phenotype and stage (all mice with that stage): {'DPR': {'early': 1.48, 'late': 1.88}, 'PR': {'early': 2.11, 'late': 2.78}, 'PS': {'early': 0.9, 'late': 1.25}}
PR: 3 mice with both stages, early 1.68, late 2.85, change 1.17, paired t p = 0.19
DPR: 7 mice with both stages, early 1.55, late 1.88, change 0.33, paired t p = 0.3
PS: 7 mice with both stages, early 0.77, late 1.13, change 0.36, paired t p = 0.4

In the RI60 scores PR mice with both stages rise more (1.17 z, 3 mice) than DPR mice (0.33 z, 7 mice), and no group's change has p below 0.05. This gives no sign of the slower DPR rise across RI60 that the claim describes, though with 3 PR mice it has little power.

Result: not reproduced. The DMS score is ordered as the paper describes (mean PR 2.35, DPR 1.66, PS 1.05 z), but the phenotype effect has likelihood ratio p = 0.100, and neither stage alone is significant (one-way ANOVA p = 0.124 early, 0.270 late; no Tukey pair below 0.05). The score rises from early to late in the 17 mice with both (mean 0.49, paired p = 0.046; model stage p = 0.088). With the authors' processing without the dropout step the phenotype p is 0.389. RI30 sessions, part of the paper's test, are not in the dandiset, and the mice with a DMS score differ from Figure 3E's (early PR 7, DPR 9, PS 14 against 7, 9, 15; late PR 4, DPR 7, PS 10 against 5, 6, 13), so the comparison with F2,33 is not like for like.

Result: partially reproduced. Pooling early and late pairs (reading a) gives r = 0.170, p = 0.24, n = 49; late pairs (b) r = 0.014, p = 0.95; early pairs (c) r = 0.375, p = 0.045, n = 29. Only reading (c) is positive and significant, and its r is below the tolerance around 0.53. The support is weak: corrected for the three readings, (c) has p = 0.13, and without the dropout step it gives r = 0.362, p = 0.053. The dropout step leaves out more than 1% of samples in only one DMS session of the 51 behind these pairs (1.61%), but a small fraction can still decide a session's score: the step moves 88.239 from 0.09 to 1.92 (1.61% left out), 048.392 from 0.02 to 1.81 (0.12%), 346.394 from 0.00 to 1.10 (0.55%) and 92.246 from 0.04 to 0.30 (0.70%), as dropouts of |z| above 1000 dominate the z-score.

def r_ci(df, x, y):
    d = df.dropna(subset=[x, y])
    r = stats.pearsonr(d[x], d[y])
    ci = r.confidence_interval(0.95)
    return f"95% interval of r {ci.low:.2f} to {ci.high:.2f} (n = {len(d)})"

Result: reproduced. The late DMS score does not correlate with omission time (r = 0.014, p = 0.96, n = 12); pooled early and late r = -0.050, p = 0.80. With 12 mice the 95% interval of r runs from -0.56 to 0.58, so the test cannot exclude the paper's r = 0.1 or a moderate correlation either way.

Result: not reproduced. The pooled DLS score correlates with shocks received (r = 0.326, p = 0.024, n = 48), where the paper finds none (r = -0.01). Late pairs alone give r = 0.374, p = 0.10, and early pairs r = 0.103, p = 0.60. Without the dropout step the pooled r is 0.113, p = 0.45, so the result depends on how the artifacts are handled (without it, late r = 0.033 and early r = 0.182, both p > 0.3). The dropout step is a choice made here, not in the Methods or the authors' code.

Optogenetic cohorts¶

Optogenetic mice carry no phenotype in the dandiset; they are classified here with the Methods rule from their early and late probes.

In [34]:
def opto_tables(experiment):
    s = sessions[sessions.subject_experiment == experiment]
    probes = seiler.probe_table(s, events, training_stages=("RI60",))
    el = seiler.early_late(probes).join(s.drop_duplicates("subject").set_index("subject")[["subject_arm", "sex"]], how="right")
    el["pheno"] = [seiler.classify(e, l) if pd.notna(e) and pd.notna(l) else None for e, l in zip(el.early, el.late)]
    omf = s[s.stage == "omission"].sort_values("start_ts").groupby("subject").asset_id.first()
    el["omission_min"] = [seiler.omission_time_min(events[omf[x]]["events"]) if x in omf.index else np.nan for x in el.index]
    el["n_ri60"] = s[s.stage == "RI60"].drop_duplicates(["subject", "start"]).groupby("subject").size().reindex(el.index).fillna(0).astype(int)
    el["did_not_learn"] = el.index.map(opto_subj.set_index("subject").did_not_learn)
    return s, probes, el

opto = {e: opto_tables(e) for e in ["Opto-DMS-Excitatory", "Opto-DLS-Excitatory", "Opto-DMS-Inhibitory"]}
for e, (s, probes, el) in opto.items():
    print(f"== {e}: {len(el)} mice")
    print("Mice per arm and sex:", el.groupby(["subject_arm", "sex"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0).to_dict("index"))
    print("Probe days per mouse:", probes.groupby("subject").size().value_counts().sort_index().to_dict(),
          "; days with two files holding shocks:", int((probes.n_with_shocks > 1).sum()))
    print("Training days before early / late probe:", probes[probes.probe == "early"].train_days_before.describe()[["min", "50%", "max"]].to_dict(),
          probes[probes.probe == "late"].train_days_before.describe()[["min", "50%", "max"]].to_dict())
    print("Mice with both probes:", int(el[["early", "late"]].notna().all(axis=1).sum()), "; with an omission probe:", int(el.omission_min.notna().sum()))
    print("Mice missing a probe:", el[el[["early", "late"]].isna().any(axis=1)][["subject_arm", "early", "late", "n_ri60", "did_not_learn"]].to_dict("index"))

fig5f-dms-chr2-escalation¶

Mice receiving DMS dopamine terminal stimulation on rewarded nosepokes (ChR2) escalate their nosepoking faster than EYFP and ChR2 Scrambled controls during FR1 and RI30.

In [35]:
def escalation(experiment, ref="ChR2"):
    s = sessions[(sessions.subject_experiment == experiment) & sessions.stage.isin(["FR1", "RI30"])].sort_values("start_ts")
    s = s[~((s.arm == "Unknown") & s.duplicated(["subject", "start"], keep=False))].drop_duplicates(["subject", "start"])
    rows = []
    for r in s.itertuples():
        ev = events[r.asset_id]["events"]
        if isinstance(r.side, str):
            pokes = seiler.active_pokes(ev, r.side)
        else:  # FR1 on both nosepokes
            pokes = np.concatenate([seiler.active_pokes(ev, "left"), seiler.active_pokes(ev, "right")])
        rows.append({"subject": r.subject, "arm": r.subject_arm, "stage": r.stage, "rate": len(pokes) / (seiler.session_length(ev) / 60.0)})
    d = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    d["idx"] = d.groupby(["subject", "stage"]).cumcount() + 1
    out = {}
    for st in ["FR1", "RI30"]:
        x = d[d.stage == st]
        fit = smf.ols(f"rate ~ idx * C(arm, Treatment('{ref}'))", x).fit()
        slopes = {a: np.polyfit(x[x.arm == a].idx, x[x.arm == a].rate, 1)[0] for a in sorted(x.arm.unique())}
        inter = {k.split("T.")[1].rstrip("]"): (fit.params[k], fit.pvalues[k]) for k in fit.params.index if k.startswith("idx:")}
        others = [a for a in sorted(x.arm.unique()) if a != ref]
        f2 = smf.ols(f"rate ~ idx * C(arm, Treatment('{others[0]}'))", x).fit()
        k2 = [k for k in f2.params.index if k.startswith("idx:") and others[1] in k][0]
        out[st] = {"slopes": slopes, "interaction_vs_ref": inter, "sessions": len(x), "mice": x.subject.nunique(),
                   "other_pair": (f"{others[1]} vs {others[0]}", f2.params[k2], f2.pvalues[k2]),
                   "sessions_per_mouse": (x.groupby("subject").size().min(), x.groupby("subject").size().max())}
    return d, out


def escalation_mixed(d, ref="ChR2", re_formula="~idx"):
    """Variant: a mixed model with a random intercept and slope per mouse (or, with re_formula=None, an intercept only).
    The fit's warnings are returned with it, as they bear on how far its p values can be trusted."""
    out = {}
    for st in ["FR1", "RI30"]:
        x = d[d.stage == st]
        with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
            warnings.simplefilter("always")
            try:
                m = smf.mixedlm(f"rate ~ idx * C(arm, Treatment('{ref}'))", x, groups=x.subject, re_formula=re_formula).fit(reml=False)
                out[st] = {k.split("T.")[1].rstrip("]"): (round(m.params[k], 3), round(m.pvalues[k], 4)) for k in m.params.index if k.startswith("idx:")}
                out[st]["converged"] = m.converged
                out[st]["random effects covariance"] = np.round(np.asarray(m.cov_re), 4).tolist()
                others = [a for a in sorted(x.arm.unique()) if a != ref]
                m2 = smf.mixedlm(f"rate ~ idx * C(arm, Treatment('{others[0]}'))", x, groups=x.subject, re_formula=re_formula).fit(reml=False)
                k2 = [k for k in m2.params.index if k.startswith("idx:") and others[1] in k][0]
                out[st][f"{others[1]} vs {others[0]}"] = (round(m2.params[k2], 3), round(m2.pvalues[k2], 4))
            except Exception as e:  # report a failed fit, do not hide it
                out[st] = {"failed": repr(e)}
        msgs = pd.Series([str(w.message).split("\n")[0] for w in caught if not issubclass(w.category, (RuntimeWarning, FutureWarning))])
        out[st]["warnings"] = msgs.value_counts().to_dict()
    return out

Result: not reproduced. In the pooled fit of the criterion no ChR2 slope differs from a control slope (FR1 interaction p = 0.63 and 0.98; RI30 p = 0.82 and 0.49), and the pooled FR1 slope of ChR2 mice (0.011) is not above the controls'. Per-mouse slopes tell a different story for FR1: the ChR2 median is 0.657 nosepokes/min per session, above EYFP (-0.021, p = 0.015) and ChR2 Scrambled (0.275, p = 0.021); in RI30 they do not differ (p = 0.6 and 1). ChR2 mice nosepoke more during RI30 (mean 7.75 per minute against 4.01 and 4.21). The pooled fit mixes mice with 1 to 13 FR1 sessions, so the two approaches disagree. A mixed model with a random intercept and slope per mouse agrees with the per-mouse slopes: in FR1 the ChR2 slope is above ChR2 Scrambled (difference 0.419, p = 0.034) and EYFP (0.697, p = 0.0075), in RI30 it is not (p = 0.68 and 0.70). That FR1 fit is weak evidence: it converged only after a retry with lbfgs, warns that the MLE may be on the boundary, and its random intercept variance is near zero (0.0001). A mixed model with a random intercept only puts the FR1 ChR2 slope above neither control (p = 0.46 and 0.33). Under the random slope model the criterion's rule would give partially reproduced; the criterion fixed the pooled fit before the analysis, so the outcome stays.

fig5i-dms-stim-no-omission-effect¶

In [40]:
def omission_anova(el):
    x = el.dropna(subset=["omission_min"])
    print(x.groupby("subject_arm").omission_min.agg(["mean", "std", "size", "min", "max"]).round(2).to_string())
    an = stats.f_oneway(*[g.omission_min for _, g in x.groupby("subject_arm")])
    kw = stats.kruskal(*[g.omission_min for _, g in x.groupby("subject_arm")])
    print(f"One-way ANOVA: F = {an.statistic:.2f}, p = {an.pvalue:.3g}; Kruskal-Wallis variant p = {kw.pvalue:.3g}")
    return an

Result: blocked (data missing). The dandiset holds 13 NpHR, 13 NpHR Scrambled and 16 EYFP mice, where Figure 6F counts 16, 15 and 16. The shortfall (3 NpHR, 2 NpHR Scrambled, 0 EYFP) equals the mice the paper drops (about 4 NpHR and 2 NpHR Scrambled) less the one NpHR mouse that is deposited and flagged as not learning (270.476, no RI60 session). So the dropped mice are, with that one exception, not in the dandiset. The "Did Not Learn" flag also marks an EYFP mouse that reached RI60 (244.465, 8 RI60 sessions, no probe), so it is not the paper's dropout criterion, and no file says which group (1 or 2) a mouse is in. Under the criterion the claim is blocked, as the dandiset does not say which mice were dropped.

RI30: F test of all arm x index terms p = 0.117

Result: not reproduced. In FR1 the ChR2 Scrambled slope (0.087 nosepokes/min per session) is below the EYFP slope (0.224; interaction p = 0.013; all three groups F test p = 0.034). ChR2 does not differ from either control (p = 0.12 and 0.98), and in RI30 no pair differs (p = 0.09 to 0.92). The difference is between the two control groups. A mixed model with a random intercept and slope per mouse finds no difference in slope in any pair (p = 0.43 to 0.96; FR1 EYFP vs ChR2 Scrambled p = 0.76), but its FR1 fit warns that the random effects covariance is singular, so these p values are weak evidence. A mixed model with a random intercept only fits without warnings and also finds no FR1 difference (EYFP vs ChR2 Scrambled p = 0.23, ChR2 against the controls p = 0.057 and 0.26). The FR1 difference rests on the pooled fit the criterion fixed.

Data outside the dandiset¶

figs3ab-dat-protein-not-reduced¶

Heterozygous DAT-IRES-cre mice do not have reduced DAT protein in DMS or DLS compared with wild-type mice.

The dandiset holds the western blot images (one per condition) and names the densitometry table on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.11266654) as its supplement. The table is read from Zenodo here.

In [49]:
zen = requests.get("https://zenodo.org/api/records/11266654", timeout=60).json()
print("Zenodo record:", zen["doi"], "version", zen.get("metadata", {}).get("version"), "; files:", [f["key"] for f in zen["files"]])
xl = requests.get(zen["files"][0]["links"]["self"], timeout=60).content
print("Densitometry.xlsx md5:", hashlib.md5(xl).hexdigest(), "(Zenodo checksum", zen["files"][0]["checksum"] + ")")
sheet = pd.read_excel(io.BytesIO(xl), header=None)
blocks = {}
for i, label in sheet[0].items():
    if isinstance(label, str) and label.startswith(("Female", "Male")):
        rows = sheet.iloc[i + 1:i + 8]
        blocks[label.strip()] = pd.DataFrame({"sample": rows[0].str.strip().values, "corrected": rows[7].astype(float).values,
                                              "sheet_ratio": rows[8].values})
print("Blocks in the table:", list(blocks))
print("Header row and the first block as read (rows i to i+7, columns 0 to 8):")
first = [i for i, l in sheet[0].items() if isinstance(l, str) and l.startswith(("Female", "Male"))]
print(sheet.iloc[:first[0]].to_string())
for i in first:
    print(sheet.iloc[i:i + 8, :9].to_string())
dat_rows = []
for region in ["DLS", "DMS"]:
    act, dat = blocks[f"Female {region} Actin"], blocks[f"Female {region} DAT"]
    ratio = dat.corrected.values / act.corrected.values
    geno = np.where(dat["sample"].str.startswith("WT"), "WT", "het")
    pct = 100 * ratio / ratio[geno == "WT"].mean()
    print(f"{region}: computed DAT/actin equals the sheet's ratio column: {np.allclose(ratio, dat.sheet_ratio.astype(float))}")
    for s_, g, p in zip(dat["sample"], geno, pct):
        dat_rows.append({"region": region, "sample": s_, "genotype": g, "pct_of_wt": p})
dd = pd.DataFrame(dat_rows)
print(dd.groupby(["region", "genotype"]).pct_of_wt.agg(["mean", "std", "size"]).round(1).to_string())
for region in ["DMS", "DLS"]:
    x = dd[dd.region == region]
    t3 = stats.ttest_ind(x[x.genotype == "het"].pct_of_wt, x[x.genotype == "WT"].pct_of_wt)
    mw = stats.mannwhitneyu(x[x.genotype == "het"].pct_of_wt, x[x.genotype == "WT"].pct_of_wt)
    print(f"{region}: het vs WT unpaired t = {t3.statistic:.2f}, p = {t3.pvalue:.3g}; Mann-Whitney p = {mw.pvalue:.3g}")
print("WT sample labels (one reads 'WT 4' where the others read 'WT F'):", sorted(dd[dd.genotype == "WT"]["sample"].unique()))
print("Male samples in the table:", int(dd["sample"].str.contains(" M ").sum()))

Claims that cannot be tested¶

  • figs1a-shock-aversive (Figure S1A, fear conditioning in 13 wild-type mice): the dandiset holds no fear conditioning sessions or freezing scores; every subject belongs to the fiber photometry, the three optogenetic experiments, or the western blot.
  • figs3cd-open-field (Figure S3C-D): no open field tracking is in the dandiset.
  • fig3c-gcamp-in-dopamine-neurons (Figures 3C and 4C): no histology images or cell counts are in the dandiset.
  • fig3e-ri30-dms-peaks: no RI30 photometry (see above).

How the analysis differs from the paper's. Statistics are run in Python, not Prism: mixed-effects analyses are linear mixed models with a random intercept per mouse, and two-way repeated measures ANOVAs use complete cases. Training files with no active nosepoke and no reward are left out (20 RR20 files that hold port entries only, and one 170 s false start); other files count as sessions even when a mouse has two on one day. Shock probe days with two files use the last file; mice with one probe day enter only the analyses that need that probe. Photometry follows the authors' MATLAB code, with one added step that leaves out channel dropouts (shown without it as a variant; fig4g turns on it, and fig3f and fig3g weaken without it), and only early and late RI60 sessions are available, so the RI30 stage of Figures 3F and 4F is missing. Optogenetic mice are classified with the Methods rule, as the dandiset stores no phenotype for them. The definitions of the wait after reward, extra nosepokes and nosepoke escalation are chosen here from the Results' wording. The supplementary figure legends were not available.

What was found about the dandiset. The dandiset holds operant behavior for four experiments, fiber photometry for RI60 and RR20 sessions, and western blot images. Missing against the paper: photometry during RI30 and the shock probes; 3 of 9 RR20 mice; 6 of 39 DMS excitatory mice and 5 of 47 DMS inhibitory mice; one or both shock probes of several mice; the fear conditioning, open field and histology data; any marker of the inhibitory experiment's groups 1 and 2. 20 RR20 training files of four mice hold port entries only, and several mice have two or three RI60 files on one day. The dropped DMS inhibitory mice are, but for one, not deposited. The 'Unknown' DLS excitatory files repeat sessions deposited under the named arms, and one mouse (290.407) is filed under two experiments. In left-side shock probes the reward series is named right_reward_times. One stitched photometry session mixes MedPC and TDT clocks. Several photometry recordings hold dropouts that dominate a z-score. Fiber coordinates are stored without the signs of the Methods. The fiber photometry mice carry their phenotype in the file names and notes, which made Figure 2 testable; one stored label (048.392) disagrees with the stated rule by one shock.
